lines.text: She walked *past the lifts.*
Straight to the glass doors.
At the front desk she stopped and slid the key card across the marble, slowly, the way he had slid it to her.
*“For Room 714,”* she told the receptionist. *“Tell him thank you. Tell him no.”*
Then she pushed through the doors into the warm night and did not look back.
The car park smelt of dust and diesel and somebody’s suya.
She sat behind the wheel and let her hands shake until they had finished shaking.
Seven floors up, a man was waiting for a girl who didn’t exist anymore.
She wound every window down and drove.
Harmattan air poured in, dry and cool, lifting the hem of the red dress around her knees.
The city went past in long gold streaks. Her heart was racing, *and it wasn’t fear.*
She turned the radio up. An old highlife song. She sang every word, loud and badly, *alone.*
The wind found her neck, her shoulders, all the bare skin the dress left open, *and she let it.*
She had forgotten her body could feel this alive with nobody touching it.
Not Chris. She knew that now, the way you know a door is locked.
But not the old silence either. Not one more night of it.
*She was done being quiet in her own house.*
The flat in Gwarinpa was dark. NEPA had taken the light again.
The generator droned outside. Femi was asleep on his side of the bed, his phone still glowing on his chest.
She stood in the bedroom doorway in the red dress. The same doorway he had stood in that night.
She switched on the bedside lamp. *“Femi. Wake up.”*
He squinted at her. At the dress. *“What time is it? Did something happen?”*
*“Yes,”* she said. *“Something happened. Sit up.”*
He sat up. She sat on the edge of the bed, close enough to touch, not touching.
Her voice came out steadier than she expected.
*“I have been lonely in this house for three years.”*
He opened his mouth. She lifted one hand.
*“Don’t fix it. Don’t tell me you’re tired. Just listen to me.”*
And for the first time in a very long time, *he did.*
She told him about the anniversary. The plates she washed alone. The nights she talked to the ceiling.
She told him about the 2am call, the dinner, the key card she gave back.
She watched every word land on his face. She didn’t look away.
He was quiet for so long the generator sounded loud.
*“I didn’t know,”* he said. Then, softer: *“No. I didn’t look.”*
It wasn’t a promise. *It was the first true thing he had said to her in years.*
*“I don’t know what we are now,”* she said.
*“Neither do I,”* he said. *“But I want to find out. If you’ll let me.”*
*If.* She liked that the word was hers.
The next weekend she booked a hotel room in Wuse. *One guest.*
High up, with a wide window over the whole city.
She told Femi exactly where she was going. *And she went anyway.*
She wore the red dress. She zipped it up herself, slowly, watching the mirror the whole way.
She ordered her own dinner. Pepper soup and a glass of red wine. *Exactly what she wanted.*
Nobody to wait for. Nobody to perform for. Nobody to please but her.
Later she ran a bath so hot the mirror disappeared.
She let the dress fall where it fell and sank in up to her shoulders.
She traced her own collarbone with one wet fingertip, slow and curious, *as if meeting someone new.*
Wrapped in the hotel robe, she stood at the window, barefoot.
Abuja glittered below her, every light a small promise.
Her reflection looked back from the glass: thirty-one, bare-faced, *wide awake.*
For years she had waited to be seen. By Femi. By Chris. By anyone.
Tonight, for the first time in years,
*she was the one looking.*
*And she liked what she saw.*
Lily chose Lily.

She walked past the lifts. ❤️

Lily · Part 4, the finale. She gave back the key card. She drove home with the windows down, woke her husband, and said the thing she had swallowed for three years: “I have been lonely in this house.”

Then she booked a room for one, in the red dress, and ordered exactly what she wanted.

For the first time in years, she was the one looking.
